To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

anti-HEV IgGs are more often found in HIV-infected persons than in uninfected controls, that the prevalence of anti-HEVs in HIV-infected individuals is higher than in the uninfected population, and that the prevalence of chronic HEV infection in HIV-infected subjects is low.

the Wantai assay detected more frequently anti-HEV IgGs in a German cohort than the MP assay, that the risk of developing chronic hepatitis E virus infection in HIV-infected individuals is very low in the era of antiretrovial therapy, and that the large variability in hepatitis E virus seroprevalences rates determined by different commercial assays requires consideration for diagnostic workup of hepatitis E virus infection.
26% of HIV-positive patients had anti-HEV antibodies, and 1.6% were positive by another commercial assay.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of HEV assays that are more sensitive and specific and allow a more accurate determination of the prevalence of HEV infections.
the development and validation of methods for the detection and characterization of hepatitis E virus ( HEV ) in humans.
the development of new methods for the diagnosis of viral hepatitis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HEV seropositive HIV patients are not at an increased risk to develop HEV infection.
there is no evidence for chronic hepatitis E in HIV-infected individuals in Europe.
there is no indication that HEV takes chronic course in HIV patients receiving antiretrovirus treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a high seroprevalance rate of hepatitis E virus (hepatitis E) in HIV-infected individuals, but the risk of developing chronic hepatitis E infection is very low.
we found that 26% of HIV-infected individuals were anti-HEV positive in Germany, and this was more frequent in individuals born in Europe.
there is no indication for routine screening of HIV-infected individuals for HEV antibodies in the absence of acute symptoms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the seroprevalance rate of HEV in HIV patients depends strongly on the assay used, and that the risk of HEV infection in HIV patients is very low in the era of antiretrovial therapy.
HEV infection is rare among HIV-infected individuals.
HEV seropositivity is common in HIV patients, and that this is not a sign of chronic infection, but a sign of previous exposure to HEV.
